rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the products formed when benzaldehyde reacts with the following reagents (Any two) :
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) in presence of dilute NaOH
(ii) \(\mathrm{H_2N-OH}\) in presence of weak acid
(iii) Tollen's reagent
rows.solution:
(i) WITH ETHANAL AND DILUTE ALKALI — a CROSS ALDOL ADDITION.

Benzaldehyde has NO \(\alpha\) hydrogen, so it cannot supply the carbanion and can act only as the ELECTROPHILE. Ethanal has \(\alpha\) hydrogens and supplies it. Only one product is therefore possible, where a cross aldol between two enolisable partners would give four:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH(OH){-}CH_2{-}CHO}\)

The product is 3-HYDROXY-3-PHENYLPROPANAL — the ALDOL itself. Note it is not the condensation product: dilute alkali WITHOUT heating stops here. Warming would eliminate water and give cinnamaldehyde.

(ii) WITH HYDROXYLAMINE in weak acid. It condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{H_2N{-}OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH{=}N{-}OH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is BENZALDEHYDE OXIME. A WEAK acid is specified because the reaction needs a compromise: some acid to activate the carbonyl, but not so much that the hydroxylamine is protonated and stops being nucleophilic.

(iii) WITH TOLLENS' REAGENT. The aldehyde is oxidised while silver ion is reduced to the metal, depositing a bright mirror:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + 2[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^+ + 3\mathrm{OH^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5COO^-} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\downarrow + 4\mathrm{NH_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The products are the BENZOATE ION, the reagent being alkaline, and metallic silver.

rows.stem: The conductivity of 0.001M acetic acid is \(7.8 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\). Calculate its degree of dissociation if \(\Lambda^\circ_m\) for acetic acid is \(390\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).
rows.solution:
First find the molar conductivity from the measured conductivity. The factor of 1000 converts litres to cubic centimetres, \(\kappa\) being per centimetre while the concentration is per litre:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{\mathrm{C}} = \dfrac{7{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-5} \times 1000}{0{\cdot}001}\)

\(\Lambda_m = 78\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The degree of dissociation is the ratio of this to the limiting value:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{78}{390}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}2\), that is 20% dissociated

The ratio must lie between 0 and 1, which is the check on the arithmetic. A value of 0.2 is what one expects of a weak acid at this dilution — most of the acid is still present as undissociated molecules, and the figure would rise further on diluting.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Why are melting points of transition metals high ?
(ii) Why the transition metals generally form coloured compounds ?
(iii) Why \(\mathrm{E^\circ}\) value for \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}\) couple is highly positive ?
rows.solution:
(i) Because of STRONG METALLIC BONDING, arising from their UNPAIRED d ELECTRONS.

The melting point measures how firmly the lattice holds together, and in a transition metal the unpaired d electrons take part in the metallic bond ALONGSIDE the \(s\) electrons. Far more electrons are therefore involved than in a main-group metal, where only the outermost \(s\) and \(p\) electrons are available.

The trend within the series follows: the more unpaired d electrons, the higher the melting point. Chromium, with six, is among the highest; zinc, with none, is the lowest and melts at only 693 K.

(ii) Because of D-D TRANSITIONS.

A ligand field splits the five d orbitals into two sets of different energy. An electron absorbs a photon of VISIBLE light and jumps from the lower set to the upper, and the colour seen is what remains of the white light after that absorption.

The jump needs BOTH an electron in the lower set and a vacancy in the upper — which is why \(d^0\) ions such as \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) and \(d^{10}\) ions such as \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) are colourless, having nothing to promote or nowhere to promote it to. The COLOUR depends on the size of the splitting, which is why the same metal gives different colours with different ligands.

(iii) Because reducing \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) REACHES the stable half-filled configuration.

Manganese(III) is \(3d^4\), and gaining one electron gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — every orbital singly occupied, spins parallel, an arrangement of unusual stability.

A species strongly inclined to be REDUCED has a large positive reduction potential, and manganese's is \(+1{\cdot}57\) V, much the highest of the \(\mathrm{M^{3+}}/\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) couples in the series. Manganese(III) is correspondingly a powerful oxidising agent and disproportionates in water.

rows.stem:
(a) Using valence bond theory, predict the hybridization and magnetic character of the complex : \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) (Atomic number : Ni = 28)
(b) Write IUPAC name of \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2\,Cl(NO_2)]}\).
(c) Why \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) is a more stable complex than \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) ?
rows.solution:
(a) Nickel is atomic number 28, and carbon monoxide is a NEUTRAL ligand in a neutral complex — so nickel is in the ZERO oxidation state, \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^8 4s^2\).

Carbon monoxide is a STRONG field ligand. It drives the two \(4s\) electrons into the \(3d\) set, giving \(3d^{10}\): every electron PAIRED and no \(3d\) orbital vacant.

Bonding must therefore use the \(4s\) and all three \(4p\) orbitals, giving \(sp^3\) hybridisation and a TETRAHEDRAL shape. With no unpaired electron the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

The contrast with \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) is worth holding: same geometry, same \(sp^3\), but nickel there is \(+2\) with two unpaired electrons, so that complex is paramagnetic.

(b) Fix the oxidation state first. The two ammines are neutral, the chlorido gives \(-1\) and the nitrito gives \(-1\), and the complex as a whole is NEUTRAL — so platinum must be \(+2\).

Ligands are named in ALPHABETICAL order regardless of charge, and the "N" records which atom of the ambidentate nitrite is bonded to the metal:
DIAMMINECHLORIDONITRITO-N-PLATINUM(II)

There is no counter ion to name, the complex being neutral, and no \(-\mathrm{ate}\) suffix, which belongs only to anionic complexes.

(c) Because of the CHELATE EFFECT.

Ethane-1,2-diamine is BIDENTATE: it binds the cobalt through BOTH of its nitrogens at once, closing a FIVE-MEMBERED ring. Three of them close three such rings. Ammonia is MONODENTATE and closes none, although six of them supply the same six donor atoms.

Two reasons make the chelate the more stable. Once one nitrogen has attached, the second is held close to the metal and binds readily, whereas a separate ammonia would have to arrive from solution. And releasing a chelating ligand requires TWO bonds to break at once rather than one, which is far less likely.

There is a thermodynamic way of putting the same point: three ligands replacing six increases the number of free particles in solution, so the ENTROPY rises and the reaction is favoured.
